title: an argument for the sake of heaven
hook: a holy book that writes down its arguments, and keeps the losing side
carry: argue to learn, not to win
tomorrow: the man who argued with God about Sodom

segments.voice: Yesterday: mitzvah, a responsibility that becomes yours. Your line was it's yours now. Six words this week: the mezuzah, the candles, mensch, seder, the glass, mitzvah. Today, the seventh.
screen: `MEZUZAH · CANDLES · MENSCH · SEDER · THE GLASS · MITZVAH`

segments.voice: Open a page of the Talmud, the great library of the rabbis' discussions, and you'll find something you might not expect in a holy book: arguments. One rabbi says this. Another says no, that. Then a third weighs in. And very often the side that lost is written down too, and kept, for centuries. A holy book that saves its disagreements.
screen: `A PAGE OF THE TALMUD.` → `ONE SAYS THIS, ONE SAYS THAT.` → `THE LOSING SIDE, KEPT.`

segments.voice: Machloket means a disagreement. And there's a famous pair at the center of it: Hillel and Shammai, two great teachers about two thousand years ago, and the schools of students who followed them. You met Hillel on day three. The two schools argued for years, about prayer, about Shabbat, about how to live. Finally, the story goes, a voice from heaven settled it: both of these are the words of the living God. And the law follows Hillel. Wait. Both are right, but one wins? Why Hillel? Because, the story says, his students were kind and humble. They taught Shammai's view along with their own, and even taught Shammai's first. An old teaching names the difference between a good argument and a bad one. An argument for the sake of heaven will last, and its example is Hillel and Shammai. An argument to win, to beat someone, won't. Remember the slanted mezuzah from day one: an argument where nobody had to lose. So when Jews argue over a text, often out loud, in pairs, across a table, it isn't a lack of faith. It's how people learn.
screen: `MACHLOKET — A DISAGREEMENT.` · `HILLEL AND SHAMMAI.` · `BOTH ARE THE WORDS OF THE LIVING GOD.` · `FOR THE SAKE OF HEAVEN.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. First breath: someone you disagree with. Second breath: the best version of their side, put as fairly as you can. Third breath: notice that you can hold it without letting go of your own.
Machloket. A disagreement, and in this tradition a way of learning: argued for the sake of heaven, with both sides kept. Seventh word: a week's worth.
Your line: argue to learn, not to win. That's week one: seven words, and what's inside each. Tomorrow, a man who argued with God himself.

screen: `DAY 7 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE MAN WHO ARGUED WITH GOD ABOUT SODOM.`

howItsDone: Jews study the Talmud and other texts in pairs (chavruta) or in groups, arguing out loud over the meaning; the Talmud records majority and minority opinions side by side, and its discussions are studied in yeshivas, synagogues and daily study programs.

fork.setup: two schools have argued for years. a voice from heaven says both are the words of the living God. whose view becomes the law?
options: neither; the argument goes on forever.
fork.reveal: Hillel's, the story says, because his students were kind and humble, and taught Shammai's view, even before their own.

original.note: Hebrew: a disagreement, from a root meaning to divide, or share out.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jews just like to argue.
what it means: disagreement as a way of learning, argued for the sake of heaven, with both sides kept.

what a scholar hears: Eruvin 13b, elu va-elu divrei Elohim chayim, these and these are the words of the living God; Avot 5:17 sets Hillel and Shammai as the argument for the sake of heaven, and Korah's rebellion as the other kind.

story.title: the oven, the tree and the voice
story.text: A rabbi is losing an argument about whether a certain oven can be used, and he's sure he's right. If I'm right, he says, let this carob tree prove it, and the tree tears itself out of the ground. Let the stream prove it, and the water flows backward. Finally a voice from heaven announces that he's right. The other rabbis still won't budge: the Torah is not in heaven, one of them says; it was given to people to work out. Later, the story goes, God laughed and said: my children have won.
story.source: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 59b (the oven of Akhnai)

wrong.myth: arguing about religion means you don't really believe.
wrong.truth: in this tradition it's a way of learning. the Talmud keeps both sides, even the one that lost.

notes: New lesson 2026-10-06 (research: 'why Jews argue about the text', the proposed day 7). Kept light and story-led; the Talmud is named once and described in plain words, per the research's warning against leading with it as 'the hard scholarly text'.
Eruvin 13b says the schools argued for three years; told as 'for years'. The reasons (they were kind and humble, taught both views, and Shammai's first) are paraphrased. Confirm.
Hillel and Shammai dated 'about two thousand years ago' (late first century BCE to early first century CE); confirm the hedge.
Avot 5:17: the argument not for the sake of heaven is Korah and his company; glossed in the spoken text as 'an argument to win'. Confirm.

Story (Bava Metzia 59b): told up to 'my children have won' (Elijah reports God smiling, 'My children have defeated Me'). The story continues with Rabbi Eliezer's excommunication, which is not told. Confirm the cut and the wording 'won'.
